📌 Bonding Curves: How Token Prices Move With Every Buy and Sell

Main Points
⏺ Bonding curves define a token’s price as a math function of supply
⏺ Every buy pushes the price up along the curve; every sell pushes it down
⏺ This post explains why bonding curves are popular for launches and micro-caps

1️⃣ Core Concept — instead of an order book, a smart contract sets the price based on how many tokens are already minted or held.
2️⃣ Automatic Pricing — early buyers get cheaper tokens; as demand increases, the curve raises the price automatically.
3️⃣ Liquidity Built-In — the contract always stands ready to buy back tokens along the same curve, so there’s no traditional LP needed.
4️⃣ Design Choices — steeper curves pump price faster but are more volatile; flatter curves are smoother but less “explosive.”
5️⃣ Risks — thin real liquidity, manipulation, and the fact that math-driven pricing doesn’t guarantee real fundamental value.

Final Thoughts

Bonding curves turn token price into a formula instead of a market guess — transparent, but still only as meaningful as the demand behind it.

MOU by Threats: Iran’s Version of “Peace”

The Swiss technical talks ended the way this whole war has gone: with a neat joint statement stapled over a fistfight. On paper, everyone smiles. In practice, Iran and the US walk away telling completely different stories about the same 80 minutes in a room.

From Tehran’s side, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi sells it as a clean win. The US Office of Foreign Assets Control issues a general license for Iranian oil and petrochemicals. Twelve billion dollars in frozen assets are to be released in two tranches. 

A “safe passage” mechanism is set up in the Strait of Hormuz, a “de‑confliction unit” in Lebanon, and four working groups begin their slow dance on nuclear issues, sanctions, and disputes. This is packaged for domestic consumption as Iran clawing back what was “always its own,” not receiving any gifts.

Then Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, parliament speaker and head of the delegation, tells a very different story. According to him, while they were in session, Trump was threatening Iran’s president, the negotiating team, and the country itself with new strikes. 

Ghalibaf says he told JD Vance that Article 1 of the understanding bans threats and coercion, declared that Iran “will never negotiate under threats,” walked out — and did not come back. 

The Americans, in his version, begged for another meeting; the Iranians refused direct talks and agreed to communicate only via Qatari and Pakistani mediators. Out of that, plus 80 minutes of contact and a dramatic exit, came the “successful” joint communiqué.

The foreign ministry’s spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, lays down Tehran’s red lines in plain language. Nuclear and sanctions talks will only happen within 60 days after the preliminary clauses are implemented. 

The US has already authorized energy sales with full insurance, banking and transport. Iran demands total removal of all sanctions, not cosmetic waivers. Within 30 days of a final agreement, all US forces must leave Iran’s neighborhood, and they are barred from reinforcing in the meantime. 

Missile capabilities are “not on the table” with anyone. And whatever is being unblocked, Iran insists it is simply reclaiming what sanctions stole.

Meanwhile, the choreography around the paper tells its own story. Ghalibaf heads to China to lock in another pole of support. Above the Persian Gulf, five US KC‑135R tankers and two KC‑46A Pegasus aircraft circle — a flying reminder that Washington still intends to supervise implementation with fuel lines and AWACS, not only with signatures. 

Reuters reports Marco Rubio struggling to sell nervous Gulf monarchies on re‑engaging Tehran under this new architecture, torn between cheap oil, fear of Iran, and distrust of Trump’s staying power.

And in Tehran’s studios, a new line is drawn: an IRIB host declares that from now on, chanting “Death to America” or burning US flags is forbidden and will be met with arrests. 

The regime that built its identity on ritualized hatred is suddenly instructing its citizens to mute the chant, not because it loves Washington, but because it has just discovered that “Death to America” doesn’t mix well with billion‑dollar oil waivers and asset releases.

Washington says it is building oversight mechanisms on Iran. Tehran says it is embedding itself deeper into regional security, forcing the US to negotiate around its missiles, its proxies, and its geography. 

Both can claim “success” — but only because neither side is honest enough to admit what they actually signed was not peace, but a temporary trade: dollars and tankers in exchange for 60 days without open war.

🔔 Ripple targets $1B revenue run rate without counting XRP holdings 

❗️ According to posts shared by CoinMarketCap and crypto-focused accounts on X, Ripple expects to end 2026 with a $1 billion revenue run rate. The figure does not include XRP held on Ripple’s balance sheet. That detail matters because Ripple has long faced public debate over the link between its business and XRP. Garlinghouse’s target frames the company as a fintech infrastructure provider that aims to earn money from products, clients, and services, not from token holdings or sales.

🌐 The deal also supports Ripple USD, known as RLUSD. Ripple has promoted the stablecoin for enterprise settlement and collateral use. Recently, crypto news reported that Ripple is also adding RLUSD to new payment tools, including services tied to AI agents and machine payments on the XRP Ledger. Company materials point to custody, treasury management, and liquidity services as core offerings. These products target banks and firms that need faster settlement, account control, and access to digital assets through regulated processes, rather than retail trading.
